canonical_statement: ISLEND-2 evaluated whether switching virologically suppressed adults with HIV-1 from daily oral standard of care to once-weekly oral islatravir–lenacapavir maintained efficacy and safety through week 48.
ISLEND-2 was a randomised, open-label, active-controlled, phase 3 non-inferiority trial conducted at 100 sites in 14 countries and territories.

Eligible participants were adults aged at least 18 years with HIV-1 RNA below 50 copies/mL on standard of care for at least 6 months, no previous virological failure, no previous islatravir or lenacapavir exposure, and no active or occult HBV infection; pregnancy at screening or day 1 was exclusionary.

population.label: Adults with virologically suppressed HIV-1 eligible for ISLEND-2
inclusion_criteria: HIV-1 RNA <50 copies/mL on standard of care for ≥6 months
No previous islatravir or lenacapavir exposure
No serological evidence of active or occult HBV infection
exclusion_criteria: Pregnancy at screening or day 1 before study drug

canonical_statement: Participants were randomly assigned 1:1 using interactive response technology, stratified by geographical region, antiretroviral class, and screening CD4+ T-cell category; treatment allocation was not masked.

The islatravir–lenacapavir group received loading/initiation dosing on days 1 and 2 with two tablets each containing islatravir 0.5 mg and lenacapavir 300 mg, followed by islatravir 2 mg plus lenacapavir 300 mg orally once weekly from day 8 without regard to food.

canonical_statement: The comparator group continued its existing guideline-recommended oral standard-of-care antiretroviral regimen, generally once daily, for at least 96 weeks.

canonical_statement: Participants were scheduled for visits on day 1; weeks 4, 8, and 12; and every 12 weeks thereafter, and islatravir–lenacapavir adherence was measured by pill count.
The primary endpoint was the proportion of participants with HIV-1 RNA at least 50 copies/mL at week 48 using the FDA-defined Snapshot algorithm.
A secondary efficacy endpoint was the proportion of participants with HIV-1 RNA below 50 copies/mL at week 48.
Change from baseline in CD4+ T-cell count was a secondary efficacy endpoint.

concept.text: Change from baseline in CD4+ T-cell count

canonical_statement: Safety endpoints included discontinuation of islatravir–lenacapavir because of adverse events and change from baseline in absolute lymphocyte count.

outcome.definition: Included study-drug discontinuation due to adverse events and change in absolute lymphocyte count

canonical_statement: Exploratory endpoints included the HIV Participant Perspective of Regimen Change questionnaire and resistance mutations in participants with confirmed virological rebound and HIV-1 RNA at least 200 copies/mL.

Virological rebound was defined as HIV-1 RNA at least 50 copies/mL at a visit on or after day 1 confirmed at the subsequent scheduled or unscheduled visit, or as an HIV-1 RNA value at least 50 copies/mL at the last on-treatment visit in specified discontinuation or loss-to-follow-up circumstances.

A sample size of 600 participants was estimated to provide at least 93% power for the primary non-inferiority analysis, assuming 2% virological failure in each group and a 4 percentage-point non-inferiority margin.

For the primary endpoint, treatment differences and two-sided 95.002% confidence intervals were constructed using a stratum-adjusted Mantel–Haenszel proportion; non-inferiority required the upper confidence bound to be below 4%, and superiority required it to be below 0%.

Change in CD4+ T-cell count was analysed with a mixed model for repeated measures including treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction, baseline CD4+ T-cell count, antiretroviral class, and geographical region as fixed effects and participant as a random effect.

The sponsors, Gilead Sciences and Merck Sharp & Dohme, developed the protocol, collected data, monitored trial conduct, conducted statistical analyses, and were involved in data interpretation, report writing, and the decision to publish.

Of 727 screened participants, 647 were eligible, 634 were randomised, and 626 received treatment and entered the full and safety analysis sets: 314 received islatravir–lenacapavir and 312 continued standard of care.

Among 626 treated participants, median age was 52 years (IQR 42–60), 211 (34%) were assigned female at birth, 193 (31%) were Black, 119 (19%) were Asian, 123 (20%) were Hispanic or Latine, and 89 (14%) were aged at least 65 years.
At baseline, 552 of 626 participants (88%) were taking one antiretroviral pill per day and 478 (76%) were receiving an integrase strand transfer inhibitor plus one or two NRTIs.

At week 48, HIV-1 RNA was at least 50 copies/mL in 1 of 314 participants (0.3%) receiving islatravir–lenacapavir and 4 of 312 (1.3%) continuing standard of care; the adjusted risk difference was −1.0 percentage points (95.002% CI −3.0 to 1.1), meeting non-inferiority but not superiority.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that once-weekly islatravir–lenacapavir was non-inferior to daily standard of care for maintenance of virological suppression and was generally well tolerated through week 48.
The authors concluded that islatravir–lenacapavir could represent the first complete once-weekly oral regimen for HIV-1 treatment and could expand patient-centred dosing options.

Because viraemia and previous virological failure were exclusionary, the study population was likely enriched for people without major adherence challenges, limiting generalisability of the very high adherence observed.
The trial excluded people who were not virologically suppressed and those with previous virological failure, so efficacy in those populations was not established.
People with HBV infection were excluded because islatravir–lenacapavir lacks anti-HBV activity; therefore, the trial does not establish use in HIV/HBV coinfection.
The trial was not designed to study islatravir–lenacapavir in pregnancy, and contraception was recommended for participants who could become pregnant.
The open-label design could have biased reporting of treatment-related adverse events, and the authors reported no mitigation strategy for that potential bias.

Detailed adherence data on dose timing and patterns of missed doses were not collected because adherence relied on pill counts; an optional weekly reminder tool could also have modestly increased adherence in the intervention group.

Patient-preference results require caution because participants self-selected for interest in weekly therapy and the preference measure reported in this article was limited to the islatravir–lenacapavir group.
The primary report presents week-48 outcomes; the authors stated that longer-term safety and immunological follow-up to week 96 is needed.
ISLEND-2 was funded by Gilead Sciences and Merck Sharp & Dohme as part of a collaboration between the two companies.

The declaration of interests reports multiple financial relationships between investigators and HIV-drug manufacturers; several authors were employees and shareholders of Gilead Sciences or Merck Sharp & Dohme/Merck & Co.

The protocol and statistical analysis plan are provided in the appendix, and Gilead Sciences states that anonymised individual-patient data may be shared with qualified external researchers upon request subject to company review and stated conditions.

One participant receiving islatravir–lenacapavir became pregnant, delivered at 33 weeks after hospitalisation for worsening glycaemic control, and the infant had reassuring Apgar scores; one participant receiving standard of care became pregnant and had a spontaneous abortion.
